practice.unfiltered: Filtration removes solids from a wine before bottling, and in doing so it can strip out yeast and bacteria as well. A wine bottled unfiltered has skipped that step, which leaves more in suspension and leaves the wine less stabilised than it would otherwise be. Two things the flag does not tell you: unfiltered is not the same as unfined, since fining is a separate process a producer may still have used, and a sediment in the bottle is a consequence of the decision rather than a fault. The flag is drawn from each producer's own published material rather than an audit, an inspection or a certification, and in this guide it is currently recorded in the Adelaide Hills.
practice.unfined: Fining clarifies and stabilises a wine by adding an agent that binds to suspended matter and carries it out of solution; a wine described as unfined has simply skipped that step. Because several of the traditional fining agents are animal derived, unfined wines are often suitable for vegans, though not always, and the flag on its own does not prove it. Unfined is also not the same as unfiltered, and this guide records the two separately, so a wine may be one, both or neither. The flag is taken from each producer's own published material rather than from an audit, an inspection or a certification; within this guide it is currently documented in the Adelaide Hills, by a single published producer.
practice.wild_ferment: Wild ferment, also called native, ambient, spontaneous or indigenous ferment, means the winemaker does not inoculate with a cultured yeast strain and instead lets the yeast population already present on the grapes and in the winery begin the fermentation. It is slower and less predictable than an inoculated ferment, which is the whole of what the term describes. It is a single technical decision in the cellar; it is not a certification, and it proves nothing about anything else the producer does with the fruit. This guide records the practice only where a producer states it in their own published material, so the flag is a record of a claim rather than an audit or an inspection, and it currently appears against entries in the Adelaide Hills and the Yarra Valley.

region.adelaide-hills: Adelaide Hills is a registered region of South Australia, sitting within the Mount Lofty Ranges zone and taking in towns from Norton Summit, Summertown and Piccadilly in the west through Hahndorf, Woodside and Lobethal to Gumeracha, Birdwood and Harrogate further out. It carries two registered sub-regions of its own, Lenswood and Piccadilly Valley, so a label bearing either name is pointing at a boundary rather than a district in loose trade use. One caution for anyone reading labels closely: the region's town of Mount Barker shares a name with the registered Great Southern sub-region in Western Australia, and the two are unrelated. The published entries here name chardonnay, pinot noir, gamay, cabernet sauvignon, merlot and petit verdot.
region.yarra-valley: The Yarra Valley is a registered Australian geographical indication within the Port Phillip zone, in Victoria, taking in a spread of towns from Lilydale, Coldstream and Yarra Glen through to Healesville, Seville, Hoddles Creek, Warburton and Yarra Junction. Labels and conversation often divide it into the Upper Yarra and the Lower Yarra, and it is worth knowing that neither is a registered sub-region; those names describe a habit of trade rather than a boundary anyone has drawn on the register. Among the producers documented here so far, the varieties named are chardonnay and pinot noir.

state.SA: South Australia's registered wine regions run from the Barossa Valley and Eden Valley north of Adelaide to the Clare Valley and the Southern Flinders Ranges, west to the Adelaide Plains and The Peninsulas, south through the Adelaide Hills, McLaren Vale, Langhorne Creek, Currency Creek, the Southern Fleurieu and Kangaroo Island, inland to the Riverland, and down to the limestone country of Coonawarra, Wrattonbully, Padthaway, Mount Benson, Robe and Mount Gambier. That is nineteen registered regions. Of them, this guide currently documents producers in the Adelaide Hills alone. The varieties named in those published entries are cabernet sauvignon, chardonnay, gamay, merlot, petit verdot and pinot noir.
state.VIC: Victoria's twenty-one registered wine regions run from the Murray Darling and Swan Hill in the state's north-west, through the central goldfields country of Bendigo, Heathcote and the Pyrenees, east to the Alpine Valleys, Beechworth, Rutherglen and Gippsland, and south to the cooler coastal and near-Melbourne regions of Geelong, the Macedon Ranges, the Mornington Peninsula, Sunbury and the Yarra Valley. The Grampians and Henty sit in the west, with the Goulburn Valley, Upper Goulburn, Strathbogie Ranges, Glenrowan and the King Valley filling the state's centre and north-east. Of those, this guide currently documents producers in the Yarra Valley alone, and the varieties named in those published entries are chardonnay and pinot noir. The remaining regions are registered boundaries the guide has not yet covered.

subregion.piccadilly-valley: Piccadilly Valley is a registered sub-region of the Adelaide Hills, in the hills immediately east of Adelaide, taking in the settlements of Piccadilly, Summertown, Carey Gully and Uraidla. Because it is a sub-region under the geographical indication system, the name on a label corresponds to a mapped boundary rather than to loose local usage, and a wine carrying it has to come from within those lines. The varieties named in the published entries here are chardonnay, pinot noir and gamay.

variety.cabernet-sauvignon: Cabernet Sauvignon is a cross of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc, often shortened to Cabernet on labels and lists. It ripens late and needs a long season to get there, which is why the Australian regions best known for it are the cooler and more maritime ones. In this guide, the producers working with it are documented in the Adelaide Hills.
variety.chardonnay: Chardonnay is a white grape handled in many different ways in Australia, from unoaked and early-picked through to barrel-fermented and matured on lees, which means the label and the winemaking notes matter more than the variety name alone. It is also a principal grape in traditional-method sparkling wine, so a bottling under this name may be still or sparkling. In this guide it is currently documented in the Adelaide Hills and the Yarra Valley, across three published producers.
variety.gamay: Gamay, also known as Gamay Noir, is a red grape grown in Australia only in small plantings, found in the Yarra Valley, the Adelaide Hills, Mornington Peninsula and Tasmania. It is often made with whole bunches in the ferment. In this guide it is currently documented in the Adelaide Hills.
variety.merlot: Merlot is a black grape that ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon, which is one reason the two are so often blended, and it is planted across most Australian wine regions. That breadth means it turns up both as a component in a Bordeaux-style blend and as a wine bottled under its own name. Within this guide, the entries recording Merlot currently sit in the Adelaide Hills.
variety.petit-verdot: Petit Verdot is a red Bordeaux variety that, in its home region, often struggles to ripen before the season closes. It has no such trouble in warmer Australian conditions, and is grown in the Riverina, the Riverland and Margaret River. It is planted both as a blending component and as a variety bottled on its own. In this guide, the producers currently documented working with it are in the Adelaide Hills.
variety.pinot-noir: Pinot Noir, often shortened to Pinot, is thin-skinned, early-budding and sensitive to site, which is why in Australia it is planted in the coolest places available and why single-vineyard bottlings are common. Sensitivity to site cuts both ways: the same trait that makes the grape difficult also makes the differences between one block and the next worth bottling separately. It is also a principal grape in traditional-method sparkling wine. Within this guide, Pinot Noir is documented in the Adelaide Hills and the Yarra Valley.
